question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with a fifteen-year history of biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis that followed three decades of heavy beer consumption but has remained clinically compensated during the past six years of complete abstinence was seen in the ambulatory hepatology suite late on a Tuesday morning for what had been scheduled as a routine surveillance visit; he came sooner than his usual six-month interval because over the previous week he noticed a vague sense of fatigue when mowing his lawn and wanted reassurance that “the liver numbers” were still stable. His background also included diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, mild hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 10 mg nightly, and remote open cholecystectomy at age 41; there had never been variceal hemorrhage, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or needle drainage of the abdominal cavity, and he had never required lactulose, rifaximin, or loop-thiazide diuretics. Medications at presentation were atorvastatin, aspirin 81 mg daily for primary cardiovascular prevention, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and cyanocobalamin 1000 µg weekly by mouth; he reported no herbal preparations, had no known drug allergies, and denied acetaminophen use in excess of 1 g per day. He lives with his spouse, walks two miles every morning, and follows a 2 g sodium diet recommended by his nutritionist, having maintained a 20-pound weight loss for four years; he never smoked cigarettes and denies any illicit drug use. Family history is notable for a father who died of myocardial infarction at 72 and a mother with rheumatoid arthritis; no relatives have chronic liver disease. Review of systems obtained prior to examination was negative for fever, chills, night sweats, right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, pruritus, lower-extremity swelling, or unintentional weight change, and sleep pattern remained normal. On arrival—before venipuncture, intravenous access, or administration of any medications—vital signs were temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. The man appeared well nourished, conversed fluently, recalled three objects at five minutes, and recited the months in reverse order without hesitation. Conjunctivae were pink and sclerae lacked icterus; oral mucosa was moist without fetor. Fewer than three spider angiomata were scattered over the anterior chest wall, palmar erythema was subtle, and the skin showed no bruises or excoriations. Jugular venous pulsation measured approximately 6 cm H₂O at 30°, carotid upstrokes were brisk, and cardiac auscultation disclosed a regular rhythm with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs were clear throughout on anterior and posterior fields. The abdominal wall was flat with an intact concave umbilicus; gentle percussion remained tympanitic across the upper and lower quadrants with no transition to dullness while he lay supine, and the tympany did not change after he rolled onto either side, nor could an impulse be transmitted across the abdominal surface even without counter-pressure. The liver edge was firm and finely nodular, palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, non-tender, and the spleen tip could not be felt. No pedal edema or sacral edema was present, and muscle bulk of the thighs and temporal regions was preserved. Neurologic survey showed intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, physiologic reflexes, normal heel-to-toe walk, and no flapping tremor after twenty seconds of sustained wrist extension. Point-of-care ultrasound performed immediately before laboratory draw demonstrated a heterogeneous, nodular hepatic parenchyma, a patent main portal vein with hepatopetal flow measuring 18 cm/s, a spleen length of 13.5 cm, and no free anechoic fluid in Morison’s pouch, paracolic gutters, or pelvis; kidneys were normal in size and echogenicity, and biliary ducts were not dilated. Capillary glucose read 108 mg/dL. Comprehensive laboratory tests obtained at that moment—prior to any vitamin K, albumin infusion, or other pharmacologic intervention—revealed white blood cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, platelet count 148 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 32 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 118 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 165 U/L, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL, serum albumin 4.7 g/dL, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.29. Alpha-fetoprotein measured 5 ng/mL, hepatitis B surface antigen remained negative, and hepatitis C antibody was negative by prior treatment-verified cure. An upright posteroanterior chest radiograph obtained without contrast displayed clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, and elevated right hemidiaphragm without pleural effusion; twelve-lead electrocardiogram captured normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute with a QTc of 418 ms and no ischemic or conduction abnormalities. No intravenous fluids, laxatives, diuretics, antibiotics, or transfusions had been given at the time these findings were documented, ensuring all clinical observations and laboratory values reflected the patient’s untreated physiologic state at presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points each for total bilirubin, albumin, coagulation status, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. At the untreated visit:
- Total bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL (<2 mg/dL) → 1.
- Albumin: 4.7 g/dL (>3.5 g/dL) → 1.
- Coagulation: INR 1.29 (<1.7) → 1.
- Ascites: absent, with no shifting dullness on examination or free fluid on ultrasound → 1.
- Hepatic encephalopathy: absent, with intact attention and recall and no asterixis → 1.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5 (Child-Pugh class A).
Final answer: 5
